AIPlanApplyRequest.description:
`POST /api/scenes/{sceneId}/ai-plan/apply` body (plan v2 §5).

The client echoes the accepted proposals (and the instruction/provider so
the audit trail matches what the user saw). No server-held list bridges
the two calls: the frontend owns the proposals until a user accepts.

``provider`` here is an **echo, not a control input**, and that distinction
is the whole reason it is a free-form string. ``AIPlanRequest.provider``
carries the pattern ``^(auto|llm|heuristic)$`` because there the client is
*choosing* a provider. Here it is *reporting* which one answered, and the
values ``generate_proposals`` actually emits are wider than that set:
``openai-compatible`` (any /chat/completions endpoint, including Ollama),
``anthropic``, ``heuristic``, ``unknown`` -- and, after a fallback, a
composite such as ``"heuristic (after openai-compatible returned nothing)"``
(``ai_plan.py:2287``).

This field carried that same pattern until it was measured against a live
Ollama run, and the consequence was total: **every apply whose proposal came
from a real model failed 422**, because the frontend echoed back exactly the
provider string the server had just handed it. Only the heuristic fallback
could be confirmed at all. Rejecting a value the server itself emitted turns
the audit trail into a trap, so the echo is bounded by length only.
AIPlanApplyRequest.title: AIPlanApplyRequest

AIPlanRequest.description:
POST /api/scenes/{sceneId}/ai-plan body.

`技术文档` reserves this slot: "AI 相关接口只保留占位" -- the AI endpoints
were to be placeholders in this phase. This is the placeholder filled in.

`provider` defaults to "auto": the LLM when ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set, and
the deterministic heuristic otherwise. Asking for "llm" without a key is an
error rather than a silent downgrade, because a demo that quietly stops
being AI is worse than one that says so.

`apply=false` activates the confirm gate (plan v2 §5): the server returns
`InterventionProposal[]` **without persisting** them, the client renders a
checklist, and the accepted subset is sent back to `/ai-plan/apply`. Default
`apply=true` keeps the pre-v2 one-shot behaviour so no existing caller has
to change.
AIPlanRequest.title: AIPlanRequest

AIPlanResponse.description:
What the AI module produced, and how.

`provider` is echoed because "which model actually generated this" is the
first question anyone will ask, and the answer must not require reading the
store.

When `apply=false` (plan v2 §5 confirm gate), `plan_id` is None, `features`
is the proposed count, and `proposals` carries the un-persisted draft list
the client echoes back to `/ai-plan/apply`. When `apply=true` the response
matches the legacy shape (`proposals` empty, `plan_id` populated).

`rejected` is additive (design §2.2): the refusals that did not survive the
constraint engine, one entry each, with a closed `reasonCode` and a
non-empty `warning`. A silently shorter `proposals` list is indistinguishable
from a provider that returned less, so a refusal is carried, never dropped.
AIPlanResponse.title: AIPlanResponse

AnsweredQuestion.description:
A planner's answer, echoed back on the next request (Phase 2 R13).

Matched by ``id``, which is derived from ``parameter`` alone, so the match
needs no server state, no sequence number and no timestamp.
AnsweredQuestion.title: AnsweredQuestion

ChatRequest.description:
One question, with the run it is about and the turns before it.

The run is sent by the client rather than looked up, because a run is not
persisted: it is recomputed on demand and lives in the browser's store. The
client already has it, and re-deriving it server-side would mean storing
run state this app deliberately does not keep (ADR-024: slider values are
per-run inputs, never persisted onto the scene).

history.description: Prior turns as {role, text}, oldest first. Last 8 are used.
history.title: History

run.description: The run result this question is about.
run.title: Run

ChatRequest.title: ChatRequest

DefaultCamera.description:
Union of §4.2.1's DDL comment and §3.2.1's API example.

``longitude``/``latitude`` are optional; the scene service fills them from
``center`` so the frontend always receives a complete camera.
DefaultCamera.title: DefaultCamera

EnvParams.description:
Scene-level *static* environment defaults (ADR-024).

Per-run user adjustments belong on the run, not on the scene -- moving a
rainfall slider must not mutate the object every plan hangs off.
EnvParams.title: EnvParams

InterventionFeature.description: One feature inside the GeoJSON FeatureCollection (§3.3.2).
InterventionFeature.title: InterventionFeature

InterventionFeatureCollection.description:
GET /api/plans/{planId}/interventions 200 body (§3.3.2).

A plain GeoJSON FeatureCollection -- handed straight to Cesium's
GeoJsonDataSource with no conversion.  ``features: []`` is a valid answer
and the frontend must still render.
InterventionFeatureCollection.title: InterventionFeatureCollection

InterventionIn.description:
A feature as supplied on create/update (§3.3.3).

``status``/``id``/timestamps are absent by design -- the service owns them.
InterventionIn.title: InterventionIn

InterventionProperties.description:
``properties`` of a returned feature.

§3.3.2's example shows only ``interventionType`` and ``style``; ``id``,
``status``, ``source`` and ``params`` are additive so the frontend can key,
filter and style without a second request.

``pinned`` is additive for the same reason, and it is carried here because
the pin state lives at the *top level* of the stored row (see
``app/services/pins.py``) and every reader of a plan goes through this
collection -- dropping it left the run-composition fallback chain in
``routers/scenes.py::intervention_features`` landing on its ``True``
default, so an unpinned row kept being scored. The default stays ``True``:
rows created before pinning existed carry no flag, and they must compose
exactly as they did then.
InterventionProperties.title: InterventionProperties

InterventionProposal.description:
One AI-proposed feature, **not yet persisted** (plan v2 §5).

The confirm gate (§5.1) presents these to the user; the client echoes the
accepted subset back to `POST /api/scenes/{sceneId}/ai-plan/apply` which
writes them through the normal plan-creation path.

Exposes `site_id`/`rationale`/`basis` as first-class fields so the UI can
render them without rummaging in `params`. Each is derived at construction
from the feature's `params` to keep a single source of truth: if `params`
is round-tripped untouched the derived view and the stored view stay in
sync. Values can be overridden on the wire, but a client that does so is
telling the server to trust its judgement -- the service only reads these
as rendering hints, never as grounding.

The four blocks below are the additive part of the design §2.2: the size
the proposal actually covers, the raw ask it came from, the constraints it
was checked against, and the parameters the run will read. ``status`` here
is the **proposal** honesty label (UPPER_SNAKE), distinct from the stored
intervention's ``draft``/``validated`` status.
InterventionProposal.title: InterventionProposal

LLMConfigRead.description: Public view of the live LLM configuration (plan v2 §9.2).
LLMConfigRead.title: LLMConfigRead

LLMConfigUpdate.description:
Writable fields (plan v2 §9.2). All optional; omitted leaves the live
value in place. Explicit empty string clears a field.
LLMConfigUpdate.title: LLMConfigUpdate

ParameterCard.description:
`GET /api/scenes/{sceneId}/parameter-card` response.

``sources`` names the rasters the numbers came from, so a reader can tell
whether they are looking at the committed analysis or a synthetic fallback
without reading any individual row. ``inputs`` echoes the four values the
caller chose (or the defaults), because a card whose inputs are not visible
cannot be compared against another card.
ParameterCard.title: ParameterCard

ParameterCardEntry.description:
One row of the card.

``key`` is stable and machine-readable; ``label`` is the human phrase. Both
are always present even when ``value`` is ``None``, so a row that cannot be
filled still appears and states why.
ParameterCardEntry.title: ParameterCardEntry

ParameterEntry.description:
One parameter the run reads for a kind, with its honesty label (§2.2).

``status`` is the assumption label (e.g. ``ASSUMPTION``) and ``source``
names where the number came from, so a proposal never carries a parameter
that cannot say what it is.

``confidence`` says how well the number is *known* (a provenance enum, not
a score): ``ASSUMED`` for a class default and for a planner's hand-set
value alike, because a planner's estimate is not more knowable than a
class default.

When a planner sets the value by hand (Phase 2 R17), ``status`` becomes
``USER_ASSUMPTION``, ``edited`` becomes true, and ``defaultValue`` carries
the class default that was replaced -- mandatory, because without it the
card cannot show what was overridden and the served value becomes
unrecoverable from the record.
ParameterEntry.title: ParameterEntry

PlanCreate.description:
POST /api/scenes/{sceneId}/plans body (§3.3.3).

Optionally carries initial interventions; they are written in the same
transaction as the plan so a plan can never exist half-populated.
PlanCreate.title: PlanCreate

PlanRead.title: PlanRead

ProjectModel.description:
One planned project's 3D presence on a scene.

A list, not two singular fields. `plan_project_url` and
`plan_project_footprint_url` described exactly one modeled project on the
whole scene, so the viewer's model handle and its project id were both
hardcoded and a second model could not appear at all -- the URLs, not the
frontend, were the ceiling.

Built server-side from `data/projects/*.json`, which is the one home for a
project's non-geometric facts. The geometry and the effects live in the same
file; this is the subset the viewer needs in order to draw it.
ProjectModel.title: ProjectModel

ProposalConstraints.description:
The constraint report carried by every proposal (§2.2).

All eleven fields have defaults: a rejection travels in
``AIPlanResponse.rejected[]`` and a client that omits this block still
parses.
ProposalConstraints.title: ProposalConstraints

ProposalQuestion.description:
One assumption a proposal rests on, and the planner's answer (Phase 2).

``scope`` discriminates the two kinds: ``PROPOSAL`` rows are properties of
one proposal (a reservoir and a paving slab have different footprints and
depths), and travel on ``InterventionProposal.questions``; ``SITE`` rows
are properties of the site and travel once per batch on
``AIPlanResponse.questions``.

``answer`` is what the planner typed. ``answered_value`` is the
**server's** parse of it, and is ``null`` when the answer is not numeric --
a client that sends a mismatched pair gets the server's number back and can
see the disagreement. The server's parse is the one that reaches ``params``.
ProposalQuestion.title: ProposalQuestion

ProposalRejection.description:
One refused proposal, in ``AIPlanResponse.rejected[]`` (§2.2).

A refusal is a first-class object, not an error: it carries the closed
``reasonCode`` so the UI can group refusals without parsing English, and a
non-empty ``warning`` that names the predicate in words.
ProposalRejection.title: ProposalRejection

ProposalRequested.description:
The model's raw centre + size ask, echoed verbatim (§2.2).

``extra="allow"`` on purpose: this block is provenance, so a key the model
sent that this schema does not name is preserved rather than dropped. It is
never used to derive geometry after validation -- ``geometry`` is what the
server produced from it.
ProposalRequested.title: ProposalRequested

ProposalSize.description:
The **served** size of a proposal (§2.2).

``cells`` is the rasterised cell count of the served geometry (holes
subtracted), ``areaHa`` the shoelace area of that geometry, and
``coverageFraction`` its share of the 17,316-cell study area.
ProposalSize.title: ProposalSize

RevalidateRequest.description:
The proposals as the client currently holds them, plus any answers.

``instruction`` is carried for the audit trail the response echoes; it does
not re-drive the model, so a revalidate cannot change which provider was
used or what it proposed.
RevalidateRequest.title: RevalidateRequest

RevalidateResponse.description:
What the edit did, split by whether it could move geometry (R15).

``geometry_affecting_parameters`` is empty on the edit path this endpoint
exists for, and it is returned as an explicit empty list rather than
omitted so the client **renders** the distinction instead of inferring it
from a missing field. ``values_affecting_only`` names the parameters whose
change touched no cell.

``explicit_storage_added_m3`` and ``net_storage_capacity_change_m3`` are
recomputed for the edited set so the consequence is visible before Apply --
and they are the *gross* and *net* figures, never conflated, because the
run's own net capacity change also credits the storage the ground gave up.
RevalidateResponse.title: RevalidateResponse

RunRequest.description:
POST /api/scenes/{sceneId}/run body -- one live simulation run.

The per-run inputs ADR-024 refused to persist onto the scene: they belong
to a run, not to the object every plan hangs off. ``plan_id`` selects the
scenario; ``None`` is a baseline run (today's land cover, no
interventions).

``plan_ids`` is the cumulative selection: every active project's plan, whose
interventions are merged into one scenario. It exists because the brief's
whole point is *cumulative* effect -- "rather than only assessing each
project individually" -- and a single-plan run cannot express that. When
both are sent ``plan_ids`` wins and ``plan_id`` is treated as its first
entry, so a single-project client and a cumulative one share one code path.
RunRequest.title: RunRequest

SandboxModifyRequest.description:
``POST /api/scenes/{sceneId}/sandbox/modify`` body.

``values`` are the input card's answers; a key left out keeps the value the
intervention already carries.
SandboxModifyRequest.title: SandboxModifyRequest

SandboxPreviewRequest.description:
``POST /api/scenes/{sceneId}/sandbox/preview`` body (Phase 4 T01).

The candidates are the ones the confirm gate is showing, in the shape
`/ai-plan/apply` would receive them; ``values[i]`` holds the input card's
answers for ``interventions[i]``, because the card changes the ledger and a
preview that ignored it would measure a different intervention than the one
about to be confirmed.

There is **no ``tideState``**: the level-pool ledger does not consume it, and
accepting an input this route ignores would imply the preview reflects the
tide. ``planIds`` are the run's toggled projects, which are prior work.
SandboxPreviewRequest.title: SandboxPreviewRequest

SandboxStageRequest.description:
``POST /api/scenes/{sceneId}/sandbox/stage`` body.

``features`` are the confirmed interventions verbatim (geometry, type,
params, style); ``values[i]`` holds the input card's answers for
``features[i]``. A key left out of ``values[i]`` is one the user handed to
the AI's estimate.
SandboxStageRequest.title: SandboxStageRequest

UnavailableProject.description:
A seeded project the viewer cannot draw, and why.

Present so an absent model reads as *a missing file* rather than as a
dataset that never held the project. Both facts are true statements about
different things, and only one of them is worth acting on.
UnavailableProject.title: UnavailableProject

info.description: Scene management and configuration module for the Hack4SDG 3D sandbox. Single data authority: all reads and writes go through this module (CLAUDE.md). Store mode is `file`; see docs/ARCHITECTURE.md (Decision 1).
info.title: SDG T1 API

get.description: Return the live config, keys stripped.

put.description:
Overwrite one or more fields on the live `settings` and persist them.

The edited fields are written to ``data/llm_config.json`` so the panel's
choices survive a restart; ``.env`` stays the deployment baseline for fields
the user never touched.

delete.description: Hard-delete one intervention from a plan (plan v2 §6.2, Decision 2).

post.description:
POST /api/scenes/{sceneId}/ai-plan -- natural language to a draft plan.

The GenAI entry point. The instruction is turned into intervention features
grounded in the area's own terrain, land cover and flood model, then (when
`apply=true`) stored through the same path as a hand-drawn feature:
`source="ai"`, every feature `status="draft"` (ADR-030), rendered by the
same intervention layer.

When `apply=false` (plan v2 §5 confirm gate), proposals are returned
**without** being written to the store. The client renders a checklist and
sends the accepted subset back to `/ai-plan/apply`.

It never invents geometry. If the analysis has not been run there is nothing
legitimate to site on, and the endpoint says so rather than guessing.

POST /api/scenes/{sceneId}/ai-plan/apply -- persist a confirmed subset.

Second half of the confirm gate (plan v2 §5). Features travel through the
same `scene_service.create_plan` path as a hand-drawn plan, so the stored
record is indistinguishable from one made through the legacy single-shot
endpoint.

Re-check edited proposals without saving them.

The confirm gate's third call: the client holds the proposals, the planner
edits a parameter, and this reports what the edit did. It persists nothing,
starts no run and calls no model, so it is safe to call on every keystroke
that changes the set.

A depth outside the accepted range is a **422**, not a constraint refusal:
the closed `reasonCode` set carries placement predicates on geometry, and a
client typo is not one of those (R20).

get.description:
GET /api/scenes/{sceneId}/buildings/{buildingId}/fit

The context of one building, the candidate changes worth considering, and
which one wins -- every delta produced by re-running the project's own storage
ledger over a modified land-class grid.

The caller states an objective and constraints. It never states a number to
apply: this endpoint computes what the change would do, and applying it stays
the existing `MassingOps` path in the viewer. That split is the whole design
(see app/services/massing_fit.py) -- the language model says what it wants,
the ledger says what it costs.

schema.title: Response Get Building Fit Api Scenes  Scene Id  Buildings  Building Id  Fit Get

post.description: The answer card, complete. Use the stream route when you want the steps.

schema.title: Response Chat Api Scenes  Scene Id  Chat Post

post.summary: Answer one question about a run

post.description:
Server-sent events, one JSON object per event:

`run_started`, `step_started`, `step_finished`, `delta`, `grounding`,
`answer`, `error`, `done`. The stream always ends with exactly one `done`.
post.summary: Answer one question, streaming the steps

get.description:
GET /api/scenes/{sceneId}/design-metrics

What the current massing does to shade and ventilation, measured from the
geometry, with every metric tied to a rule Hong Kong's own air ventilation
guidance states.

**This prints no verdict, and that is the design.** The AVA policy document
behind Hong Kong's guidance says a higher velocity ratio is the better design
but that "whether the better design option meets a standard cannot be known".
A pass/fail here would invent a standard that does not exist. The numbers are
for comparing this scheme against another one, which is Stage 3.

Every metric names its source rule. Nothing here is CFD, a comfort index, or
a daily energy balance, and each caveat says which of those it is not.

``dayOfYear`` is accepted as a spelling of ``day_of_year``, and the day is
range-checked -- see the note on the check below.

schema.title: Response Get Design Metrics Api Scenes  Scene Id  Design Metrics Get

get.description:
GET /api/scenes/{sceneId}/drainage/hourly?hyetograph_name=hko_2023_09_07

The hourly storm simulation: rain level and drainage, hour by hour.

Each hour's rain generates runoff through the project's own CN table, the
per-cell retention pools fill (a pool filled at hour 2 has less room at
hour 5), and the system's drainage capability removes standing water up to
the DSD published design standard for this catchment type (134 mm/h,
50-year rural, Stormwater Drainage Manual 2024 update) -- or up to a
caller-supplied rate, with ``drained_m3_per_hour=0`` as the no-drainage
counterfactual. The whole-simulation mass balance
(``rain_in == stored_gain + drained + standing_end``) is **enforced**, not
reported, and the final standing volume is routed once through the D8
cascade as a view of where it pools.

**Not a flood prediction.** The drainage capability is a published design
standard used as a proxy -- no pipe asset data exists for this site and
none is invented; the response says so every time.

``hyetograph`` is a comma-separated list of mm/h ("10,25,60,120");
``hyetograph_name`` names one of the cited reference storms
(``hko_2023_09_07`` | ``dsd_50y_design`` | ``black_rain_70``). camelCase
spellings of every parameter are accepted as everywhere else in this
router.

schema.title: Response Get Drainage Hourly Api Scenes  Scene Id  Drainage Hourly Get

get.description:
GET /api/scenes/{sceneId}/drainage/routed?rainfall_mm=450

The fill-and-spill routing of each cell's unstored volume down the D8 receiver
chain, with the mass-balance identity, the depression statistics and an
independent HAND cross-check reported beside the routed depth.

**Not a flood prediction.** Screening-level fill-and-spill on a
Priority-Flood conditioned surface; the level-pool ledger stays the headline
number and this is additive. When the receiver and raw surface have not been
generated the response says ``ROUTING_UNAVAILABLE`` with the command to run,
rather than failing.

``rainfallMm`` is accepted as a spelling of ``rainfall_mm`` for the same reason
as ``dayOfYear`` above: the design writes camelCase, the rest of this router
uses snake_case, and both are honoured.

schema.title: Response Get Drainage Routed Api Scenes  Scene Id  Drainage Routed Get

get.description:
GET /api/scenes/{sceneId}/heat-field?hours=9,14&day_of_year=196

The blended heat-exposure field for the current massing: the hand-authored
land-class index combined with sky view (from the massing geometry) and the
cast shadow at each requested hour.

**Heat is not a temperature.** The field is a relative 0-1 screening index,
never degrees Celsius. It is anchored to a cited air-temperature band (HKO
Lau Fau Shan station, July 2015-2024) that the 0-1 scale is read against; the
anchor is a committed file, never fetched at request time. The land-class
table is mapped through the single definition in ``_overlay_common`` -- not
copied.

The default solar day is 196 (15 July) so the shadow geometry matches the
July anchor band; the design-metrics/shade surface keeps its own 355 default.

Several hours are collapsed to a per-cell shaded *fraction* (the mean of the
binary masks), so the shadow term reads as "shaded this fraction of the
requested instants" rather than one instant's snapshot.

``dayOfYear`` is accepted as a spelling of ``day_of_year``: the codebase's
existing query parameters are snake_case while the design writes camelCase, and
accepting both means neither caller is silently served the default.

schema.title: Response Get Heat Field Api Scenes  Scene Id  Heat Field Get

get.description:
GET /api/scenes/{sceneId}/ledger

The headline number, and what the stored interventions do to it.

`bufferDeficitM3` is today's unstored water -- runoff with nowhere to go,
which is the figure the project's own glossary calls the single headline
number. `deltaUnstoredM3` is the change the active interventions make to it:
positive means worse than today, negative means better, under the same
assumed rainfall.

Pass `plan_id` to score a specific scenario; the default is the most recently
created plan. A scenario is a plan, so interventions from other plans are not
mixed in -- comparing two plans means calling this twice.

Interventions are translated into the land-class change each actually
implies and the project's own runoff/retention arithmetic is re-run over the
modified grid. Two kinds are refused with a stated reason rather than
approximated: `massing_height` is a 3D operation that changes no land cover,
and `drainage_alignment` needs pipe and outfall capacity this screening model
does not have.

schema.title: Response Get Ledger Api Scenes  Scene Id  Ledger Get

get.description:
GET /api/scenes/{sceneId}/parameter-card -- the brief's section 2 table.

The numbers a reader needs *before* trusting any result: the site's extent,
its land cover, the inputs the run assumed, and -- the rows that matter
most -- the things this project does not know. Soil group, heat preset and
tree cover carry no value and say why; they are not zeros.

A GET, because the card computes nothing the caller chose beyond the four
inputs, is idempotent, and is a read of a scenario in exactly the sense
``GET /ledger`` is. It takes the same optional parameters with the same
defaults as its sibling, so the two always describe the same scenario.

Every figure is read from the dicts ``ledger_for_scenario`` just computed
for this same request (R1). The card never re-sums the raster, so it cannot
disagree with a run: a disagreement would require one dict to hold two
values for one key.

GET /api/scenes/{sceneId}/pins -- the staged scenario, rows included.

Every row of the staged plan, pinned or not: a user who just unpinned
something needs it on screen to pin it back. Each row carries the
intervention verbatim (geometry byte-for-byte from what the panel quoted),
its ``pinned`` flag, and the provenance the row was pinned with -- absent
as ``null`` for sources that carry none, never invented here.

``status``/``warning`` state what the data is: nothing staged, all rows
unpinned (so the next run scores nothing pinned), or N of M rows entering
the next run. The footprints are raster reads at 5 m assembled by the
suggestion/catalog services, not surveyed sites -- the same disclosure the
panels show.

schema.title: Response List Pins Api Scenes  Scene Id  Pins Get

post.description:
POST /api/scenes/{sceneId}/pins -- pin one feature into the staged scenario.

The body is one plan intervention -- geometry, intervention type, params,
style -- exactly as the suggestion and catalog services emit them. It is
accepted as a plain ``dict`` deliberately: the shape is enforced by
``pins.pin`` through the same ``InterventionIn`` schema every other
intervention passes, so a pin cannot introduce a shape the run would then
silently ignore, and a malformed body surfaces that schema's own message
under 422 rather than a FastAPI body-parse error.

Pinning is idempotent by fingerprint (kind, geometry, parameters): the same
physical feature twice returns the row already there with
``alreadyPinned: true`` instead of a second polygon, which would double its
coverage in the guard while changing nothing on the grid. Unpin keeps the
row and marks it ``pinned: false``; the next run simply does not compose it.

schema.title: Response Pin Intervention Api Scenes  Scene Id  Pins Post

post.description:
POST /api/scenes/{sceneId}/pins/{featureId}/unpin -- take one out.

Idempotent by row: unpinning an already-unpinned feature repeats the same
``pinned: false`` write and returns the same acknowledgement. An unpin for a
feature that is not staged in this scene is a 404 -- the thing being removed
is not there -- and never a silent success.

schema.title: Response Unpin Intervention Api Scenes  Scene Id  Pins  Feature Id  Unpin Post

post.description:
POST /api/scenes/{sceneId}/run -- one live simulation run.

The run loop the sliders were always meant to drive (ADR-024 kept them
local-only until this existed): apply the chosen plan's interventions to
the land-class grid, re-run the project's own SCS-CN generation/retention
arithmetic at the requested rainfall, re-solve the level-pool fill, and
re-render both overlays. The response carries fresh overlay URLs (cache
busted by run id), the baseline-vs-scenario ledger, and a plain-language
explanation -- an LLM paragraph when a provider is configured, a labelled
deterministic template otherwise.

``planId: null`` is a baseline run: today's land cover, no interventions.
Send ``planIds`` to compose several projects into one cumulative scenario --
the brief's headline goal. The heavy terrain conditioning and the
sky-view/shade rasters are cached (they change with the offline scripts and
the massing respectively, never with a slider), so a run is seconds, not
minutes.

Screening-level, always: the response's ``status``/``warning`` say so, and
so do the sidecars written beside the PNGs in ``data/rasters/run/``.

schema.title: Response Post Run Api Scenes  Scene Id  Run Post

post.description:
The input card for one intervention: what the run reads, and the estimate.

An empty ``inputs`` list is an answer: the kind has no value the ledger
reads, so there is nothing to ask.

schema.title: Response Sandbox Inputs Api Scenes  Scene Id  Sandbox Inputs Post

post.description:
Change a placed intervention's values; its footprint stays where it is.

A value the run would refuse is a 422 and the sandbox is left unchanged.

schema.title: Response Sandbox Modify Api Scenes  Scene Id  Sandbox Modify Post

post.description:
What the candidates would do, measured against what is on the sandbox now.

A dedicated route rather than a `dryRun` flag on `/run`, because a run
writes overlays, prunes the run history to 20 entries, mints a `runId` and
calls a model for an explanation card -- none of which a preview may do, and
one endpoint with two shapes and different side effects is the
shape-failure class this project has already paid for twice.

Writes nothing, starts no run, calls no model. The response carries no
`runId`, no `overlayUrls` and no `explanationCard` key at all, and it labels
itself (`status` / `warning` / `scope`) in the payload rather than only in
the UI, so any other client cannot mistake these numbers for a run's.

schema.title: Response Sandbox Preview Api Scenes  Scene Id  Sandbox Preview Post

post.description:
Which placed intervention a change instruction refers to, with its card.

``isModification: false`` means the sentence does not change anything
placed, and the client treats it as an addition instead.

schema.title: Response Sandbox Resolve Modification Api Scenes  Scene Id  Sandbox Resolve Modification Post

post.description:
What a removal instruction refers to, without removing anything.

The client confirms with the user, then unpins the intervention or toggles
the project off. Resolving and acting are separate calls on purpose: a
removal is never applied on the strength of a parse alone.

schema.title: Response Sandbox Resolve Removal Api Scenes  Scene Id  Sandbox Resolve Removal Post

post.description:
Confirm interventions onto the sandbox, with the input card's answers.

The features are pinned into the scene's staged plan, the one place the
Interventions panel reads and every run composes. A value the run would
refuse is a 422 naming the field, and nothing is written.

schema.title: Response Sandbox Stage Api Scenes  Scene Id  Sandbox Stage Post

post.description:
The three suggestions shown under a run's card: one per axis.

Real footprints from the rasters, with the estimate and the input card
attached. Asked for after the run returns rather than inside it, because
ranking candidates takes seconds the run should not wait on.

schema.title: Response Sandbox Suggestions Api Scenes  Scene Id  Sandbox Suggestions Post

post.description:
POST /api/scenes/{sceneId}/scenario/compare

Rank several candidate schemes against each other under weights the *caller*
states, or refuse to rank when none are given.

Each scenario is evaluated against the **same** baseline city model -- the
shared-baseline precondition :func:`compare` relies on -- so the numbers being
ordered are genuinely comparable. The ordering is a weighted favourability
built from each axis min-max normalised *within the compared set*; it is never
a score, `combinedScore` stays null, and there is no pass/fail. The three raw
axes stay visible on every row.

Request body::

    {
      "scenarios": [
        {"scenarioId": "A", "massingOps": [...], "interventions": [...]},
        {"scenarioId": "B", "massingOps": [...], "interventions": [...]}
      ],
      "weights": {"shade": 0.5, "ventilation": 0.3, "drainage": 0.2}
    }

``weights`` may be omitted, in which case the response refuses to order. An
unknown axis, a negative weight or an all-zero vector is refused with 422, as
is an unrecognised massing scope -- never widened.

schema.title: Response Post Scenario Compare Api Scenes  Scene Id  Scenario Compare Post

post.description:
POST /api/scenes/{sceneId}/scenario/evaluate

Score a candidate scheme against the baseline on **all three axes at once**:
shade, ventilation and drainage.

**There is no combined score in the response, and that is the design.** The
units are incompatible (a fraction of ground, a dimensionless blockage, cubic
metres), the ventilation axis has no threshold to normalise against, and the
axes genuinely conflict -- raising heights shades more ground and blocks more
wind. A single number would settle that trade-off silently. The three axes
come back separately with their own units, and `tradeoffs` says in words what
moved.

Request body, all optional::

    {
      "massingOps": [{"op": "scale_all", "multiplier": 1.4, "scope": "west"}],
      "interventions": [{"kind": "green", "ring": [[lon, lat], ...]}],
      "rainfallMm": 450,
      "sunHours": [9, 14],
      "dayOfYear": 355
    }

An unrecognised scope is refused with 422 rather than widened to the whole
district: "make the western blocks taller" answered with an edit everywhere is
the failure this project has already made once.

schema.title: Response Post Scenario Evaluate Api Scenes  Scene Id  Scenario Evaluate Post

get.description:
GET /api/scenes/{sceneId}/scenarios

Brief task 9: three *real published* development programmes, encoded and run.

The figures are CEDD's own published works areas -- First Phase about 19.6 ha,
Second Phase Stage 2 about 200 ha, and all six Second Phase main works
contracts totalling about 253.5 ha. CEDD publishes no land-use allocation and
no layout, so the split of that area between bare ground and green, and its
location on the grid, are this project's assumptions and are returned with the
result rather than buried.

`areaShortfallHa` matters: where it is non-zero the district did not have
enough land of those classes to convert, so the delta is capped and
understates the real effect. For the Second Phase that shortfall is most of
the programme.

schema.title: Response Get Published Scenarios Api Scenes  Scene Id  Scenarios Get

get.description:
GET /api/scenes/{sceneId}/sea-level

The brief's task 21: run the same layout with the sea raised by the official
Hong Kong projections for 2100, and report what changes.

The numbers come from Hong Kong Observatory's *Mean sea level projection for
Hong Kong* (revised 21 Aug 2024): 37-82 cm under SSP2-4.5 and 57-108 cm under
SSP5-8.5, relative to the 1995-2014 mean. The brief's own "+0.4 m / +0.8 m"
sit inside those ranges rather than replacing them, so both are run.

**The result is that none of them changes the deficit at this site**, and the
reason is reported rather than papered over: the study area's ground runs from
2m to 141 m and the ponds are landward, so no retention surface is submerged.
The mechanism that would actually bite here is a submerged drainage outfall --
the jacking effect -- which needs a pipe network this screening model does not
have.

schema.title: Response Get Sea Level Scenarios Api Scenes  Scene Id  Sea Level Get

get.description:
GET /api/scenes/{sceneId}/suggestions -- the loop's suggest step.

Ranked candidate sites, one axis at a time, with the per-cell arithmetic
that produced each estimate. Deterministic by construction: no model, no
clock, no randomness, so the same query twice returns the same ranking.

``rainfall_mm`` is accepted so a suggestion can be read against the run the
user is actually looking at; it changes the estimates and never the
ordering of the pools.

schema.title: Response Get Suggestions Api Scenes  Scene Id  Suggestions Get

get.description:
GET /api/scenes/{sceneId}/ventilation

Air-ventilation screening by frontal area density, per wind direction.

**This is not a wind tunnel and not a CFD solve.** It is geometry: the total
building face presented perpendicular to each wind, over the site area. Low
means the wind penetrates, high means the site is sheltered from that
direction. A velocity ratio is a different quantity from a different method,
and the two are reported side by side rather than mixed.

The published reference is the AVRG73 air ventilation assessment for Hung
Shui Kiu Area 13, which states the dominant wind directions for this site are
NE, ENE and E -- together 40.8% of wind frequency. No frequency is invented
for any other direction.

No pass/fail threshold is asserted. The bands live in Technical Circular 1/06
and its Annex A Technical Guide, which this project has not extracted, and a
screening that graded itself against thresholds it had not read would be
exactly the kind of confident wrong answer this project keeps refusing to
produce.

schema.title: Response Get Ventilation Api Scenes  Scene Id  Ventilation Get

get.description:
GET /api/scenes/{sceneId}/ventilation/corridors?directions=NE,SW

The least-cost through-route across the frontal-area cost surface, per wind
direction -- the openest path the wind can take, computed from the geometry.

``directions`` defaults to the eight principal directions; the wind-direction
table is the canonical one in ``design_metrics`` (never re-derived here, which
is how NE and SW get swapped). The corridor is **geometry, not flow**: it is
not a measured wind speed and FAD is not a velocity ratio, which the response
states.

schema.title: Response Get Ventilation Corridors Api Scenes  Scene Id  Ventilation Corridors Get

get.description:
Liveness, plus the demo machine's GenAI state.

`llm` is here so that on the day, whether the demo is running a real model
or the deterministic fallback is one `curl` away rather than a surprise. It
reports *configured*, never *working* -- only a real call proves that, and
`scripts/llm_probe.py` is what proves it. Reporting a green light for an
unverified path is exactly the overclaiming the spec forbids.
